article.title: Palestinians Face Down the Israeli Genocid
article.author: Ramzy Baroud, Robert Corsini, Dick Price, Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On October 3, 2026, Palestinian American journalist, author, and historian Ramzy Baroud delivered a powerful keynote address at the Fourth Annual Left Coast Forum at California State University, Los Angeles. Speaking about Israel's genocide in Gaza and the Palestinian struggle for liberation, Baroud combined family history, anti-colonial analysis, and an urgent call for international solidarity. His central message was unmistakable: Palestinians are not simply victims of history. They are active participants in shaping it, and their refusal to disappear represents a fundamental challenge to the colonial system seeking to displace them. Ramzy Baroud: Left Coast Forum (49:29) A Sister's Life and Death Baroud began not with political theory but with the story of his sister, Dr. Suma Baroud, a physician who spent three decades delivering babies and treating the wounded in Gaza. After briefly leaving Gaza for Turkey, she returned voluntarily, compelled by her connection to her homeland and her responsibility to its people. During Israel's bombardment, she worked under devastating conditions, treating injured children without adequate electricity, medical supplies, or painkillers. In 2024, Baroud told the audience, an Israeli drone struck her vehicle as she returned from the hospital, killing her. Her story framed the central questions of his address: "Why do we stay? Why do we resist? Why do we refuse to disappear?" For Baroud, his sister's decision to remain in Gaza embodied a collective Palestinian commitment to land, community, and identity, even when remaining could mean death. Related: Beyond Israeli Apartheid: Why Britain's Greens Are Challenging Zionism Itself The Nakba Never Ended Baroud rejected the prevailing tendency to treat the destruction of Gaza as an isolated humanitarian catastrophe. Instead, he situated the current genocide within the historical continuum of the Nakba, the mass displacement and dispossession of Palestinians beginning in 1948. "The Nakba is an ongoing structural process," he declared. He traced this process through the expulsion of Palestinians from their villages, Israel's 1967 occupation, the Oslo agreements, and the prolonged siege of Gaza. Drawing on the 1923 writings of Zionist leader Ze'ev Jabotinsky, Baroud described the Iron Wall doctrine: the belief that overwhelming military superiority could eventually convince Palestinians that resistance was futile. Yet, he argued, decades of military domination have failed to extinguish Palestinian demands for freedom and self-determination. Baroud described the events beginning in October 2023 as a historic rupture that exposed the limits of military power. Whatever one's interpretation of October 7, he insisted that Palestinians must be recognized as people possessing political agency rather than merely as passive subjects of Israeli decisions. Reclaiming Palestinian History One of Baroud's strongest arguments concerned who gets to tell the Palestinian story. For generations, he observed, Palestinians have been described by colonial administrators, Western journalists, Israeli officials, and outside commentators whose interpretations frequently displaced Palestinian testimony. Even sympathetic solidarity movements have sometimes elevated outside voices over those of Palestinians themselves. Baroud called for what he termed "narrative sovereignty" : the right of Palestinians to document, interpret, and communicate their own history. He illustrated this through his family's experience. His parents came from a peasant community displaced from the village of Bayt Daras in 1948. Forced into refugee life in Gaza, they possessed few material resources, but his father insisted that education would become the family's source of strength. His sister eventually became a physician. For Baroud, such accounts are not simply family memories. They constitute a people's history that challenges attempts to erase Palestinian existence. He urged the audience to recognize the historical significance of refugees' testimonies, family photographs, village memories, and keys to homes from which Palestinians were expelled. Related: Israel Is Losing Hollywood Sumud: Survival as Resistance Baroud devoted particular attention to the Palestinian concept of sumud , commonly translated as steadfastness. But steadfastness, he explained, should not be confused with passive endurance. "Sumud is an active revolutionary strategy for survival and resistance," he said. He offered examples: a farmer replanting an uprooted olive tree, a teacher continuing lessons in a makeshift classroom, a family erecting a tent on the ruins of its destroyed home, and a doctor treating wounded patients without anesthesia. These actions, he argued, directly challenge a system that depends upon Palestinian displacement and disappearance. Drawing on Italian Marxist Antonio Gramsci's concept of organic intellectuals, Baroud also described Gaza's teachers, journalists, physicians, and mothers as individuals whose everyday work embodies political resistance. Their contributions deserve recognition alongside those of prominent political leaders and intellectuals. From Sympathy to Solidarity Turning to the international response, Baroud condemned Western governments for providing military, financial, and diplomatic support to Israel while professing commitments to human rights and international law. He contrasted those governments with the growing international movement demanding Palestinian freedom. He praised South Africa's decision to bring its genocide case against Israel before the International Court of Justice, alongside solidarity efforts across Africa, Latin America, and Europe. He also highlighted university encampments, labor organizing, weapons-factory protests, and dockworkers refusing to handle military cargo destined for Israel. For Baroud, these actions demonstrate the difference between expressions of sympathy and meaningful solidarity. Solidarity, he argued, requires shared risks and collective action. He connected Palestine's liberation struggle to the broader movements against colonialism, apartheid, and white supremacy, invoking thinkers including Frantz Fanon, James Baldwin, Malcolm X, and Angela Davis. Related: Iran War Exposing Limits of U.S. Power Building a Movement Around Principles Baroud concluded by challenging solidarity organizations to move beyond factional disputes and disagreements over political personalities. Movements, he maintained, must organize around enduring principles rather than individual leaders. Among those principles he identified were Palestinian self-determination, racial and economic equality, the right of refugees to return, and an end to settler-colonial apartheid. He also rejected approaches that focus exclusively on humanitarian relief while leaving the structures responsible for Palestinian dispossession intact. "We must stop managing the victims and start confronting the system of oppression," he told the audience. His closing challenge shifted responsibility from Palestinians, whose steadfastness he considered established, to those watching from abroad. "The question is, what will we do?" It was a fitting conclusion to an address grounded in both tragedy and determination. Baroud asked his listeners not merely to witness Palestinian suffering, but to recognize Palestinian agency and accept responsibility for translating solidarity into organized political power. For the Left Coast Forum audience, his message reached beyond Gaza: liberation requires more than sympathy for the oppressed. It demands confronting the systems that produce oppression—and joining the struggles of those determined to overcome them. Rob Corsini of Videocratic Media recorded and created the video.
